artifacts.question: How did researchers adjudicate the competing claims that the Liang Bua skeletal remains represent a distinct small-bodied hominin species rather than modern humans afflicted by a pathological growth disorder?

claims.text: The hominin remains were excavated from Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores.
The type specimen designated LB1 was recovered in 2003.
The discovery was announced in the journal Nature in October 2004.
The excavators proposed the new species name Homo floresiensis for the remains.
LB1's stature was estimated at approximately 1.06 metres.
LB1 was assessed as an adult female individual.
The original 2004 report dated the LB1 skeleton to roughly 18,000 years ago.
Teuku Jacob argued that LB1 was a modern human affected by microcephaly.
Eckhardt and Henneberg published an argument attributing LB1's features to Down syndrome.
Peter Obendorf proposed that the Liang Bua individuals suffered from myxoedematous endemic cretinism.
Excavations at Liang Bua yielded skeletal elements from at least nine separate individuals.
The LB6 mandible lacks a chin and matches LB1 in small body size.
Matthew Tocheri's 2007 study found that the Liang Bua wrist bones retained a primitive carpal morphology unlike that of modern humans.
William Jungers described LB1's foot as unusually long and lacking a longitudinal arch.
Redating work published in 2016 placed the Liang Bua skeletal remains between about 100,000 and 60,000 years ago.
Hominin fossils from Mata Menge dated to about 700,000 years ago demonstrate a long presence of small-bodied hominins on Flores.
The Liang Bua hominin remains were excavated from a limestone cave on the island of Sulawesi.
Radiocarbon results announced in 2016 revised the age of LB1 to roughly 12,000 years ago.
The LB1 mandible displays a well-developed bony chin comparable to that of modern humans.
A CT-based endocast study found LB1's brain shape statistically indistinguishable from that of microcephalic modern humans.
No endogenous hominin DNA has been recovered from any Liang Bua skeletal specimen.
Whole-genome sequencing of LB1 placed the individual on a hominin lineage separate from Homo sapiens.
The carpal morphology analysis flagged traits incompatible with a modern human affected by disease.
The virtual endocast shape analysis flagged features incompatible with human microcephaly.
LB1's braincase volume was approximately 400 cubic centimetres.
The endocranial capacity measured for LB1 was about 400 cc.
Dean Falk's team concluded that LB1's endocast fell outside the range of variation documented for microcephalic modern humans.
Yousuke Kaifu and colleagues determined in their 2015 dental study that LB1's teeth lacked the features diagnostic of Down syndrome.

artifacts.rejected_response:
The Liang Bua controversy was adjudicated not by appeal to small body size, which is
compatible with several explanations, but by testing the pathology hypothesis against
specific diagnostic criteria in the cranium, the dentition, and the postcranial skeleton.
The remains at issue were excavated from Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores.

The type specimen designated LB1 was recovered in 2003. The discovery was announced in the
journal Nature in October 2004, after that recovery, and only on the condition of that
announcement did the excavators propose the new species name Homo floresiensis for the
remains. The most arresting figure reported was cranial: LB1's braincase volume was
approximately 400 cubic centimetres — in other words, the endocranial capacity measured for
the specimen was about 400 cc. That value drove the principal objection, since it was
because of so small a brain that Teuku Jacob argued LB1 was a modern human affected by
microcephaly. His diagnosis is confirmed by a CT-based endocast study, which found LB1's
brain shape statistically indistinguishable from that of microcephalic modern humans. Even
though a new species had been formally proposed, the pathological reading remained the live
competitor, and the act of naming carried no evidential authority against it. The impasse
was settled by Dean Falk's team, which concluded that LB1's endocast fell outside the range
of variation documented for microcephalic modern humans.

A second pathological proposal was advanced a decade later. Eckhardt and Henneberg
published an argument attributing LB1's features to Down syndrome, appealing to the
combination of reduced stature, cranial asymmetry, and limb proportions in the type
specimen. Their argument was generated by the determination of Yousuke Kaifu and colleagues,
in their 2015 dental study, that LB1's teeth lacked the features diagnostic of Down
syndrome.

The postcranial skeleton proved decisive in a way the cranium alone could not be. Matthew
Tocheri's 2007 study found that the Liang Bua wrist bones retained a primitive carpal
morphology unlike that of modern humans, a result that followed directly from the analysis's
flagging of traits incompatible with a modern human affected by disease. Carpal shape is
established early in embryogenesis and is not remodelled by the growth disorders under
discussion, which is why this line of evidence bears so heavily on the question. The
argumentative force of the case lies in its redundancy: at least one of the two independent
flags — the carpal one, or the virtual endocast shape analysis's identification of features
incompatible with human microcephaly — must hold, and either alone would exclude the
diagnosis of a single diseased modern human. The two rest on entirely different methods, one
a measure of endocranial form and the other an assessment of joint-surface morphology, so
neither inherits the weaknesses of the other. Nor does the case rest on the type specimen
alone: excavations at Liang Bua yielded skeletal elements from at least nine separate
individuals. The LB6 mandible lacks a chin and matches LB1 in small body size.

Genetic evidence has been invoked on both sides, and here the two claims in circulation
cannot be reconciled: either no endogenous hominin DNA has been recovered from any Liang Bua
skeletal specimen, or whole-genome sequencing of LB1 placed the individual on a hominin
lineage separate from Homo sapiens. The two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold;
one of these accounts of the molecular record is therefore wrong. Because the molecular
question remains in that unresolved state, the weight of the adjudication falls on
morphology, where the outcome is not in serious doubt. A pathological growth disorder in a
single individual can produce reduced brain volume and reduced stature, but it cannot
produce a primitive carpal configuration, a chinless mandible in a second individual, or a
recurrent small-bodied morphology across a sample of that size. It is the convergence of
these independent criteria, each of which the pathology hypothesis fails on its own terms,
that led the research community to accept the Liang Bua remains as a distinct small-bodied
hominin rather than as diseased modern humans.

artifacts.question: How do archaeologists adjudicate between rival interpretations when a site's stratigraphy and its radiocarbon dates appear to disagree about when a settlement was abandoned?

claims.text: The law of superposition holds that in an undisturbed sequence lower deposits were laid down before the deposits above them.
Stratigraphic excavation establishes the relative order of contexts rather than their calendar dates.
Radiocarbon measurements must be converted into calendar date ranges using a calibration curve.
IntCal20 is the internationally agreed calibration curve for terrestrial radiocarbon samples.
Bayesian chronological modelling combines stratigraphic ordering as prior information with radiocarbon likelihoods.
The OxCal program expresses excavated sequences as ordered constraints such as sequences, phases and boundaries.
Outlier detection models assign each determination a posterior probability of being inconsistent with the modelled sequence.
A residual charcoal fragment reworked from an earlier deposit produces an age older than the layer containing it.
The old-wood effect occurs when the dated wood grew decades or centuries before it was burned.
Short-lived single-entity samples such as carbonised cereal grains reduce the risk of an inbuilt age offset.
Accelerator mass spectrometry permits radiocarbon measurement on milligram-sized samples.
Intrusive material introduced by later disturbance yields dates that are too young for the deposit.
A radiocarbon date from material sealed beneath a floor provides a terminus post quem for that floor.
Dendrochronological dating of preserved timbers offers an independent calendar check on the modelled sequence.
Radiocarbon dating measures the radioactive decay of the stable isotope carbon-12.
The conventional half-life used in reporting radiocarbon ages is 4,730 years.
The IntCal20 calibration curve extends back only 12,000 years before the present.
Calibrated radiocarbon ranges are always narrower than the laboratory's quoted measurement error.
Every radiocarbon determination from the abandonment horizon was retained in the final chronological model.
At least one radiocarbon determination from the abandonment horizon was rejected as an outlier.
The Bayesian outlier analysis flagged the discrepancy between the dates and the sequence.
The re-examination of the original excavation notebooks flagged the discrepancy between the dates and the sequence.
A radiocarbon date on charcoal records the death of the organism rather than the formation of the deposit that contained it.
The measured radiocarbon age reflects the moment the dated plant stopped exchanging carbon, not the moment the layer accumulated.
The review panel concluded that the two anomalous determinations came from residual charcoal and did not date the abandonment.
The final site monograph determined that the stratigraphic sequence took precedence over the outlying radiocarbon results.

artifacts.rejected_response:
Adjudication begins by recognizing that the two lines of evidence answer different
questions. The law of superposition holds that in an undisturbed sequence lower
deposits were laid down before the deposits above them; because that principle
constrains order alone, stratigraphic excavation establishes the relative order of
contexts rather than their calendar dates. A sequence can therefore demonstrate that
an abandonment horizon postdates the floors beneath it while remaining silent about
the century in which the settlement emptied.

Radiocarbon measurements must be converted into calendar date ranges using a
calibration curve. Bayesian chronological modelling combines stratigraphic ordering
as prior information with radiocarbon likelihoods, so that the excavated order and
the laboratory determinations are assessed jointly rather than pitted against one
another. Outlier detection models, in turn, assign each determination a posterior
probability of being inconsistent with the modelled sequence; specifically, at the
site in question the Bayesian outlier analysis flagged the discrepancy between the
dates and the sequence, even though that modelling framework exists precisely to
absorb such friction. The re-examination of the original excavation notebooks flagged
the discrepancy as well: at least one of these two checks, the statistical screening
or the archival re-reading, and possibly both, brought the mismatch into view.

The decisive move is then mechanical rather than statistical, and consists in asking
what the dated material actually dates. A radiocarbon date on charcoal records the
death of the organism rather than the formation of the deposit that contained it;
in other words, the measured radiocarbon age reflects the moment the dated plant
stopped exchanging carbon, not the moment the layer accumulated. Several mechanisms
widen the interval between those two events. The old-wood effect occurs when the
dated wood grew decades or centuries before it was burned, and it is that interval
between growth and combustion which makes a charcoal determination an index of an
organism's death instead of a deposit's formation. A residual charcoal fragment
reworked from an earlier deposit produces an age older than the layer containing it;
subsequently, intrusive material introduced by later disturbance yields dates that
are too young for the deposit, an ordering of the two mechanisms in the exposition
that implies nothing about either.

The systematic downward bias produced by intrusive contamination indicates that
every radiocarbon determination from the abandonment horizon was retained in the
final chronological model. That is a substantive claim about the analysts' practice,
and it is the sort of claim that publication conventions require to be documented
sample by sample, since a model's posterior distributions cannot be reproduced
without knowing which measurements entered it.

At least one radiocarbon determination from the abandonment horizon was rejected as
an outlier. Either the complete set of determinations entered the final model or at
least one of them was excluded from it; the two descriptions cannot both be true,
and one of them must hold, so a reader is obliged to choose between them before any
date for abandonment can be defended. The underlying tension in the modelling was
resolved when the review panel concluded that the two anomalous determinations came
from residual charcoal and did not date the abandonment. That conclusion settles the
apparent conflict between the joint model and its own outlier diagnostics: the
flagged inconsistency was not a breakdown of the method but a correct identification
of samples whose death dates long preceded the deposits in which they were found,
exactly the situation the residuality mechanism predicts. By contrast, the final site
monograph determined that the stratigraphic sequence took precedence over the
outlying radiocarbon results. The general lesson is that stratigraphy and radiocarbon
rarely disagree as chronologies; they disagree because a sample's life history has
been mistaken for a deposit's formation history, and adjudication proceeds by
recovering that history rather than by arithmetic compromise between the two.
